summary: Defines object identifier values that identify Ethernet chip sets for network management. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Unique ID numbers that tell what brand and kind of chip sits inside a network card.

questions: what is the ether chipset mib
how are ethernet chips identified in snmp
what is an object identifier in snmp
subtitle: A registry of ID numbers that name the Ethernet chips inside network equipment, kept for backward compatibility.

tldr.problem: Network management software wanted a standard way to report which Ethernet MAC chip an interface uses, and the list of chip identifiers had been buried inside the EtherLike-MIB.
tldr.mechanism: This memo splits those registrations into their own MIB module, ETHER-CHIPSET-MIB, which assigns an OBJECT IDENTIFIER to each chip set under dot3ChipSets, grouped by vendor.
tldr.outcome: The object that used these values, dot3StatsEtherChipSet, is deprecated, so the module only records historic assignments that old implementations may keep using.

today: RFC 2666 is an Informational memo published in August 1999 and is not obsoleted. It describes historic assignments for a deprecated object, so it matters mainly for backwards compatibility with older SNMP implementations.

sections.title: Why a Separate Chip Set Registry
sections.content:
RFC 2666 defines OBJECT IDENTIFIER values for use with network management protocols. They are meant for the dot3StatsEtherChipSet object in the EtherLike-MIB (RFC 2665), which identifies the MAC hardware used on an interface.

The registrations were split out of that MIB into a separate document for maintenance purposes. The object has recently been deprecated, so the memo's purpose is to capture historic assignments made by the IETF working groups that maintained the EtherLike-MIB.

Implementations that support the object for backwards compatibility may keep using the assigned values. For a chip set that is not listed, implementors should assign a value within the part of the registration tree delegated to individual enterprises.
sections.eli5: The old list of chip numbers got its own notebook so it is easier to keep tidy. Nobody is adding to it much any more, but old devices can still use it.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
Like other MIB documents of its era, the memo restates the SNMP Management Framework. It lists five major components: an overall architecture (RFC 2571), the Structure of Management Information (SMIv1 and SMIv2), message protocols (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3), protocol operations, and a set of fundamental applications with view-based access control.

Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store called the Management Information Base, or MIB, and objects in it are defined using the SMI. This module is written in SMIv2. An SMIv1 version can be produced by translation, and the result must be semantically equivalent except where something cannot be translated, such as use of Counter64.
sections.eli5: SNMP is a way for a manager program to ask machines about themselves. The MIB is the big list of questions it is allowed to ask, and this memo adds some answers to that list.

sections.title: The ETHER-CHIPSET-MIB Definitions
sections.content:
The module ETHER-CHIPSET-MIB is registered as etherChipsetMIB at { mib-2 70 }. It defines dot3ChipSets as { dot3 8 }, and under that node it creates one branch per manufacturer.

The vendor branches, numbered 1 to 12, are AMD, Intel, Seeq, National Semiconductor, Fujitsu, Digital, Texas Instruments, Toshiba, Lucent, Galileo, Jato and XaQTI. Each chip below a branch is an OBJECT-IDENTITY with status current and a description that calls it the authoritative identifier for that chip. For example, the AMD Am7990 LANCE is { dot3ChipSetAMD 1 }.

The module itself contains no managed objects, only identifier values for other MIB modules to use.
sections.eli5: Think of a school with twelve classrooms, one for each chip maker. Each chip gets a desk number inside its maker's room, so its full address is room plus desk.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the module defines no management objects, it has no effect on Internet security by itself. The concern is the deprecated dot3StatsEtherChipSet object, which may be sensitive in some environments: it would let an intruder learn which vendor's equipment is in use on the network.

Where the object is still implemented, it may be important to control read access to it and possibly to encrypt its values in transit. Not all versions of SNMP can do this, and SNMPv1 by itself is an insecure environment. The memo recommends considering SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575).
sections.eli5: Telling strangers exactly which brand of chip is in your computer could help a bad guy pick the right trick. So only the right people should be allowed to ask.
